en: Shi Dunlun’s *Collected Explanations of the Treatise*, Fascicle 52, Part 2:

Explaining the Equal and Immediate Condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). It says: "If these six consciousnesses [serve as the condition] for those six consciousnesses, they constitute the equal [and immediate condition]."
Regarding the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth:
there are masters in the Western Regions who, based on this very text,
establish that the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) exist as a continuous succession of multiple moments and thus possess the immediately preceding condition.

However, at the end of the *Pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says: "In a single moment, the five consciousnesses necessarily give rise to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which seeks [its objects] on the level of mind (*manobhūmi*).
It further states: "The five consciousnesses do not continue for two moments, nor do they successively produce other consciousnesses."
It should be understood that this statement is made on the basis of the *sāṃkathya-citta* (the mind of sudden occurrence);
it refers to the state prior to the arising of a continuous flow (*nisyanda*) or the grasping of another object.
The five consciousnesses continue in their own kind without interruption;
therefore, they possess an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) within their own kind.
According to the second master, the five consciousnesses necessarily do not continue in succession for more than two moments.
Following the *Maulī Bhūmi*,
one must simply understand this passage of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*:
"If these six consciousnesses serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those six consciousnesses..."
This statement is general; one should specify that it concerns the mental consciousness in relation to the six consciousnesses,
and the six consciousnesses in relation to the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the six consciousnesses in relation to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as equivalent and immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*),
I have now consulted the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla in the fourth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Each of the eight consciousnesses takes only its own kind as its opening-and-leading support (*ābhimukhya-pravartaka-āśraya*).
This is because while the wording of this treatise is general, its intended meaning is specific.
This is explained within the section on the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Briefly, six types are distinguished.
Question:
What is the difference between the fruit of the agreeable and disagreeable and the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) such that it must be further clarified?
The commentary explains:
Specifically, the distinct experiences of suffering and pleasure within the six consciousnesses, induced by wholesome and unwholesome karma, are termed "fruits of the agreeable and disagreeable.
Subsequently, the experience of neutral sensation (upekṣā) induced in the ālayavijñāna is termed the "ripening fruit" (vipākaphala).
The preceding section has completed both the headings and the explanations for the correct determination of the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
From here on is the third [section], which addresses the mutual inclusion and exclusion between the two causes, the ten causes, and the four conditions.
Regarding the statement that "the single type of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), when viewed in relation to the phenomena it produces, can act as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) and so forth":
This is the productive cause (*janakahetu*).
As stated in the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "The projecting [cause] and the producing [cause] are the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
Furthermore, the fifth fascicle states: "The producing [cause] is the causal condition, which is subsumed under the productive cause."
The twelve links of dependent origination are not [merely] projecting causes.

As stated in the tenth fascicle: "Regarding these twelve links in relation to one another, they are all explained as being based on predominance (*adhipati*) in terms of what is produced, what is projected, what is brought forth, and what is drawn in."

Therefore, there is no [separate] causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, as in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
thus, it is known that the essence of the generative cause is itself the causal condition.
Both arising (*utpāda*) and drawing forth (*ākṣepa*) are universally applicable to the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If arising were exclusively the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*),
it would contradict the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the cause for the arising of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
In this passage, it is based on the *Pañcavastuka* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, which subsume six causes; therefore, this refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and not others.
If one does not harmonize it with these [texts], [the meaning remains incomplete].
The link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), having been moistened, is itself the cause;
it is not the cause for the arising of birth and old age and death.
Therefore, there is no sense in which they arise instantaneously.
The conclusion answers the previous question to ensure it is clearly understood.
Regarding the establishment of the ten causes based on causal conditions,
this is as explained previously in the thirty-eighth [section] and the fifth.
One portion of the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
one portion of the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*) is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
and the remaining portions, as well as one portion each of the projecting and appropriating causes, are the other conditions.
These are all dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The preceding three sections have completed the definitive analysis of the four conditions.
From here on, the second section distinguishes the meaning of the mind that is unarisen through conditions.
First, the question;
second, the answer;
third, the objection.
Section Four. Question:
As the Blessed One has said, up to "for what reason is that activity taught as the condition for the arising of consciousness"?
This is the intent of the question.
According to our own school’s position, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the past and future exist as substantial entities (*dravya*) that serve as conditions for the arising of mental states.
Now, however, the Master [Vasubandhu], within the Mahāyāna school, maintains that the past and future are non-existent.
"How is it that the Buddha said past and future formations serve as conditions for the arising of the mind?
This contradicts the Sūtra, which states:
'If the mind were to arise by taking as its object a non-existent entity, and so forth.'"
This second point contradicts the Sūtra.

The answer is: because it can maintain the objects that are not within the range of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), the Blessed One metaphorically designates it as "dharmas" and so forth.
The meaning of the answer is this:
if there are phenomena that possess substantial existence (svabhāva) exclusively in the present,
they are called "real phenomena" (bhūta-dharma) because their substance exists.
If the past and future do not exist as real entities,
yet they can maintain their own non-existence, prevent the five consciousnesses from functioning, and cause the mental consciousness to arise—
then that which is metaphorically designated as "dharmas," how could this truly be dharmas?
Therefore, it is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
In the previously cited sutra, there was only the measure of the dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*) without the word "sphere" (*āyatana*);
it was a provisional designation for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
It is not because something is called a "dharma" that it is thereby subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* and must consequently possess a substantial entity (*svabhāva*).
One should establish the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*): Just as I have stated, past and future dharmas, though non-existent, should also be named "dharmas."
Because there is something apprehended,
as in the case of present phenomena,
it would follow that the mind has no object for the past, future, and so forth, as they lack substantial existence.
The mental consciousness should take an entity-less dharma as its object; because it is a dharma,
just like a dharma that possesses an entity.
In Sanskrit, *dhāra* means "to hold" (*dhṛti*) in Chinese;
in Sanskrit, *dharma* also carries the meaning of "holding. Because it is able to hold [its characteristics], it is called a "dharma" (phenomenon).
The question, "By what causes and conditions is it known that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses this intentional meaning?
constitutes the third objection. The intent of this objection is as follows:
The Buddha taught that mental consciousness arises conditioned by the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Since this sphere of phenomena must certainly exist, how is it known?

The Buddha’s teaching that past and future [phenomena] lack their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) yet cause mental consciousness to arise is a provisional designation; he spoke of them as "existent" with a specific underlying intention (*saṃdhi*).
In the fourth section below,
first there is a correct response based on principle;
second, there is again the citation of extensive discourse to prove that consciousness arises dependent [on conditions].
Regarding the preceding section:
first, an example is raised as a response.
This refers to that mental consciousness up to those [factors] which are not objects of that [consciousness], and are subsumed under the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
You previously cited a sutra stating that mental consciousness arises conditioned by the mind and dharmas;
you thus insist that there must definitely exist dharmas within the sphere of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*).
Yet, we clearly observe that the mind and consciousness take past and future [objects] as their conditions.
How could it be said that the consciousness which takes [past or future objects] as its object is included within the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana)?
Although past and future consciousnesses serve as objects for the mind (manas), one must not insist on classifying them as the sphere of mental phenomena based on the sūtras.
Furthermore, although past and future phenomena are objects of the mind, one cannot maintain that these phenomena exist as real entities based on the sūtras.
One should establish the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"The various phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are the objects of the mind in the two periods of the past and the future."
It is apprehended in an improper manner because it takes the consciousness of the past and future as its object and because it is the domain of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is like the six consciousnesses taking the objects of the past and future.
Question: Is this the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)? Answer:
The image must necessarily be comprised within consciousness alone across the three periods of time.
Therefore, this is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not a phenomenon that exists as cause and effect;
rather, it is the reflected image (*pratibimba*) that can constitute cause and effect.
Now, this is refuted according to the externalist positions.
It is not the case that within the Mahāyāna the images do not exist such that the various consciousnesses could function toward them.
Furthermore, regarding those who maintain that there is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they establish the meaning of existence and the capacity to sustain the meaning of existence, and so forth.
He demonstrates the correct principle.
If one were to raise further objections regarding the two types mentioned below:
If, regarding the two categories of existence and non-existence, one were to understand only existent phenomena and not non-existent ones,
then it would be incorrect to say that the mind takes all objects as its conditions;
for since it would only take existents as its conditions, this would contradict reason.
If you were to make such a claim, it would contradict your own *siddhānta*.
For if you say that the mind takes only existent phenomena as its object and does not take non-existent ones,
this contradicts your own school’s tenet that the mind takes all things as its object.
This constitutes the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet (*siddhānta*). *Siddhānta* is here translated as "tenet," while one interpretation renders it as "teaching" (*śāsana*).
Furthermore, one should not say "below," as that would be a contradiction and an error. Therefore, from here on:
The formation of conditions is not existent.
The Dharma Master Jeong of Silla said:
"The Dharma has three meanings."
First, the distinction of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-viśeṣa*),
as in the preceding passage concerning the meaning of the non-activity of the maintaining consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Second, the self-nature of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-svabhāva*).
As stated in the text in sequence: furthermore, that which possesses intrinsic nature (svabhāva) establishes the meaning of existence and is able to maintain the meaning of existence;
that which lacks intrinsic nature establishes the meaning of non-existence and is able to maintain the meaning of non-existence.
All [these] give rise to understanding through the three modes of engagement with phenomena (*dharmas*).

Next, the text states: "By means of that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), if a certain meaning is established regarding the nature of existence (*sadbhāva*), then by that very meaning one gives rise to a consciousness that discerns it; if a certain meaning is established regarding the nature of non-existence (*asadbhāva*), then by that very meaning one gives rise to a consciousness that discerns it."
From here below is the second section, which cites extensive discourses to prove that there is cognition of the non-existent.
This section contains two parts.
First, five types of discourse and reasoning are presented to prove that cognition has no [external] object.
Regarding the various interpretations in the subsequent commentaries on the sutras:
as for the first point of discussion mentioned above, Jing says that this "selflessness" (anātman) is not subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
because the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The conditioned and the unconditioned are called "existence.
That which is neither self nor belongs to a self is called "non-existence.
When it is said that the consciousness which contemplates the common characteristics of existence does not arise without taking those objects as its cognitive domain, [it means that it does so].
This meaning of selflessness is universally termed the "common contemplative mind-object"; therefore,
one should know that the mental consciousness can arise by taking this contemplation of selflessness as its object.
If it is produced through hearing and reflection,
it is inference (anumāna).
Regarding the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā), there are two explanations within its sphere of mind.
First interpretation:
Before entering meditative observation,
one should practice the method of contemplating non-self within the mind through hearing and reflection.
This common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely inference (*anumāna*);
when one correctly enters the contemplation of non-self through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Although direct perception individually realizes the selflessness of all phenomena, it is termed "common" from the perspective of skillful means;
this is one interpretation.
Alternatively, it refers to the wisdom of cultivation directly realizing selflessness.
This is indeed a distinct proof regarding the objective sphere of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

However, because all phenomena resemble one another in their lack of self (*anātman*), they are called "having a common basis. This means that the substantial reality (*svabhāva*) of this non-self does not exist.
Just as with correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
one realizes suchness (*tathatā*) by taking that non-apprehension as its object;
just as with preparatory knowledge (*prayogajñāna*).
There is indeed an image; one must necessarily rely on the original object. If there were no image, it would be a false claim to say that one exists.
Now, by means of the original object, I refute the opponent.
If the reflected image is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
by which nature is it subsumed? Answer:

Among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*), those subsumed under the "homogeneity of phenomena" (*dharma-sabhāgatā*) refer to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of a mind that is of the same species as that mind;
this is termed "homogeneity of phenomena."

It is not meant to say that when wisdom relying on a non-existent object illuminates the essential nature and does not give rise to further conceptualization, it is therefore subsumed under "non-existence";
this should be understood in the same way as before. As for what is called the "contemplation of common characteristics" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa):
This is stated with reference to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Alternatively, it is called "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*) because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is shared by all phenomena;
it does not mean that the cognizing mind relies upon what is shared.
Furthermore, because this contemplation is performed upon subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna), it is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
Regarding the second discussion, Jing states that it takes as its object the non-substantiality of designations such as food, drink, armies, and forests.

[This refers to] knowing each [object] individually as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Ji says: "As for what is called 'contemplation of the specific characteristic,' it is not the specific characteristic among the specific and common characteristics;
this is a general term where 'specific' is spoken in reference to the common."
"Self-nature" refers to its own essential characteristic;
that is, the specific characteristic of food and drink.
It is not like the self-characteristic of objects known by each of the five consciousnesses.
If one says that there is no self because the Truth of Suffering is the object-condition [of the cognition of "no-self"], and thus the Truth of Suffering itself is no-self,
then this would mean that while suffering exists and can be designated as such, the self does not exist.
But if one takes all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as the object-condition for the cognition of no-self, where would this [cognition] be included?
Therefore, one should know that regarding each and every non-existent object as a condition, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) should be established as follows:
"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should arise with respect to an immaterial object."
Because it is apprehended by the mind,
just like [the notion of] non-self and so forth.
Regarding the third discourse, it refers to wrong view which denies the existence of giving and other such acts.
In reality, this non-existence does not exist.
Now, arising conditioned by non-existence—
would this not be birth from conditions that are non-existent?
Regarding the statement that there is "no giving and no affection," Tai (Tai-zu) says that when parents give things to their children and so forth, it is called "affection.
The Tripitaka Master provides three explanations,
as recorded previously in the seventh [section].

Regarding the fifth discourse, it says: "In future formations, one does not fail to contemplate their arising and ceasing. Tai [Xuanzang] comments: "This also means that one contemplates the characteristics of the mind, wherein the characteristics of birth and death are present."
This is because it reveals that there is no basis for arising and ceasing;
it is also the mind that takes non-arising as its object.
If one were to take future arising and ceasing as an object, [it would not be such a mind].
This refers to the arising of the mind conditioned by [the object].
Ji says that here, the objective essence (*bimba*) is likewise non-existent.
Now, this refutes what is not Mahāyāna; furthermore, within the mental image (*pratibimba*), the mind itself does not transform into characteristics such as arising and ceasing.
One should formulate the formal argument as follows:
Past and future [phenomena] must be without arising,
because they are not subsumed within the present.
Like the horns of a rabbit and so forth,
the two periods of past and future necessarily do not have cessation,
because they lack arising.
It is like the hair of a tortoise and so forth.
Below, this connects to alternative explanations from the sūtras;
there are three such sūtras.
This explains the purport of the answer in the first sutra:
the Buddha taught that past karma already arisen perfumes the seeds within consciousness,
thereby generating those [seeds] capable of perfuming.
It is said that there is past karma;
Maheśvara is the Maheśvara of the fourth dhyāna;
and *prakṛti* is the *prakṛti* of the Sāṃkhya school.
The "Self" (puruṣa) refers to the Ātman of the Vaiśeṣika school and others.
As stated in the second sūtra:
"One should not assert that [the Self] exists by virtue of its nature of coming and going."
The substantial entities of past and future dharmas exist as present realities according to the Hīnayāna; therefore,
one should not speak of them as "past" or "future."
Since the nature of the past and future must have existed previously,
one should not use the nature of the past and future to explain their present existence.
This explains the third sutra.
Once the fruit has already been produced, the continuity of the seed-series persists;
although the capacity for the root has ceased,
the capacity to produce its own kind still continues to exist.
Having been grasped, that which has already exhausted its capacity to produce a fruit is called the past element (*dhātu*).
The seeds for the production of future fruits continue to flow in the present.
That which is called the future realm has not yet completed its present fruit;
because it has not yet bestowed its fruit, it is called the present realm.
Tài says: "If the continuity of the seeds of form that have already yielded their fruit is called the past realm (*atīta-dhātu*);
if the continuity of the seeds that have not yet yielded their fruit and will do so in the future is called the future realm (*anāgata-dhātu*)."
If the present continuity has not yet yielded its fruit,
the world considers it to necessarily perish when its own kind of seeds are exhausted;
thus, because the fruit arises, the cause ceases.
If a past fruit were to arise in the present,
it would not be a present seed.
Another explanation states:
According to the *Anuvartananyāyamukha*,
based on the meaning of the six or seven fruits associated with other categories,
it is because the cause ceases and the fruit arises.
If the seeds are present,
they likewise do not yield fruit.
This concludes the fifth major section, clarifying the meaning of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
At the end of the second fascicle of the *Manobhūmi* (the "Mind Section") within the *Maulī Bhūmi* (the "Basic Section"), it says:
"Briefly stated, there are eighty-seven dharmas within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whether provisional or substantial:
fifty-three are mental concomitants (*caitasika*)."
Form is of two kinds:
form consisting of restraint and non-restraint,
and form produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are twenty-four dissociated [factors], namely:
acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth.
There are eight unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [phenomena].
This refers to space and so forth;
detailed, they are eight, and abbreviated, they are six.
They are equal and perfectly equal.
Now, in this definitive analysis, there are only twenty-two non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);
excluding non-concordance (*aprāpti*) and spatial location (*deśa*).
Below, they await the completion of their conditions.
The following clarifies the definitive analysis of the two concentrations (*samāpatti*).
Why is it not stated that they are "not conjoined spatially" (*dig-viyoga*)?
It is because space is primarily distinguished by way of form (*rūpa*).
In terms of the disintegration of the various conditions that do not harmonize as a composite,
the characteristics of matter and mind are not manifested; therefore,
they are omitted here and not discussed.
Furthermore, I shall now briefly analyze this by means of five gates.
First, regarding the nature [of these phenomena]: they are all provisional dharmas and lack intrinsic substance.
Not only seeds, but also the formations dissociated from mind (viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha) are subsumed under the dharma-element (dharma-dhātu) and the dharma-base (dharma-āyatana).
This is a designation based on states.
Second, the explanation of the name:
in full, it should be called "non-material, non-associated formations."
The term "non-form" (arūpa) serves to exclude form (rūpa).
The term "dissociated" (viprayukta) [serves to exclude associated phenomena].
Furthermore, they are distinguished from the mind;
since the mind is associated [with mental factors], those which are not mind are therefore called dissociated.
Practice simplicity and non-action.
The dharma of non-action is also not something that can be attained through association;
rather, because it is conditioned, it constitutes practice.
Thus, they are designated by names derived from their numerical distinctions;
these specific names may be understood from the text itself.
Third, the establishment of the states of mind and matter is explained.
The third consists solely of the mental factors (*caitta*) established upon the basis;

that is to say, the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*). This is because these are designated upon the seeds where the mind is absent.
If, prior to entering the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the preceding mind perfumes and forms seeds,
and based on these seeds there is the provisional establishment of the "retribution of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*) from the perspective of the non-arising of a contrary mind.
It is also established based on those very seeds that lack maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"The three types are established based on the distinctions of the various states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)."
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"The retribution of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is established upon the ālayavijñāna; this corresponds to the retribution of conceptualization (saṃjñi-samāpatti)."
The fifty-third [chapter] states: "It is said that when mind and mental factors arise, they perish;
this refers to the perishing of the faculties, the mind, and mental factors.
Four [of these] are established solely on the basis of matter."
This refers to the sets of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya), as well as their arrangement.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"The sets of names, phrases, and phonemes are established based on the situational aspects of verbal expression."
Regarding the pervasive presence of cause and effect throughout the ten directions, one speaks figuratively of "directions.
It should be understood that herein only those causes and effects subsumed under the category of form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are discussed;
for immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*) lack the functional capacity to pervade spatial locations.
The remaining seventeen types of faculties are provisionally established based on the states of the causes and effects of form and mind.
Among them, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya),
if it is based upon the eighth consciousness, is also mental in nature.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it is established as being determined within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
which thus encompasses both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Question:

If length and shortness are established based on form (*rūpa*), they are still form. Why is it that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*), which are conventionally established based on sound (*śabda*), are not considered sound? The explanation is as follows: Name, phrase, and phoneme are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) based upon sound; they do not have the nature of sound itself. Just as length and shortness are designated in dependence upon the aggregation of atoms of form, yet are not themselves form, so too names, phrases, and phonemes are designated in dependence upon the aggregation of sound-constituents (*dhvani*), yet they are not themselves sound. Furthermore, while sound is a physical phenomenon (*bhautika-rūpa*) belonging to the aggregate of form, names, phrases, and phonemes belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as mental factors (*caitta*). Therefore, although they rely on sound for their manifestation, they are distinct from sound.
Length and shortness are established solely on the basis of form (*rūpa*);
furthermore, they are characteristics of form,
and their substance is itself form.
Names and so forth are established based on sound according to this region for the time being;
they apply universally across the ten directions and not merely to form.
Question:
If that is so, since direction is designated solely in relation to form (*rūpa*), why is it not itself form?
The explanation is as follows:
By taking all sentient beings within the directions as a whole, the four aggregates and so forth are established as the directions;
therefore, they are not form (*rūpa*).
Fourth, the three natures are clarified as being either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The substance of the maturation of non-conception is exclusively indeterminate;
the substances of the two mindless attainments are exclusively wholesome;
and the substance of the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) pertains to both the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified.
Since the seeds to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) include both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*),
it is likewise possible that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), names (*nāman*), and phrases (*pada*), etc., may also be wholesome or unspecified.
Because it is established based on form (*rūpa*).
This refers to its essential nature (*svabhāva*);
the others pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Tài says that according to the Abhidharma,
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), and names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) are neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
The fruition of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika-vipāka*) is neutral as acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta*).
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is said to be "of its own nature" (svabhāva) because it is exclusively a fruit; it is not called "attained at birth" (upapatti-labdha).
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the faculties (indriya), and the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava).
The attainment of cessation is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
the others are both tainted and untainted.
The fifth [section] clarifies their affiliation with the three realms.
The attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) are exclusively bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

As for the three—name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*)—those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are bound to the realms of desire and form (*kāma-rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is bound to all three realms;
the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is exclusively unbound;
and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) are bound to all three realms as well as unbound.
The remaining fifteen contaminated [dharmas] are bound to the three realms, while the uncontaminated are unbound.
If explained according to their basis,
they exist only in the realm of form.
The analysis of the five gates is concluded.
Within this, nineteen dharmas are briefly explained,
divided into fourteen sections.

the first is the discernment of their characteristics.
Second, the resolution of objections through explanation;
third, the distinction between the names and meanings of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Within the first [section], there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
That which was previously called "aging" and subsequently termed "abiding" is in fact the very time of arising;
it is not that it becomes different only because of the presence of abiding.
Furthermore, because it is intended to engender revulsion, the "abiding in difference" (anyathābhāva) is explained first,
as it might otherwise be confused with eternal phenomena (*nityadharma*). The answer consists of four parts.
First, there is no future birth;
second, there is no present birth;
third, it is understood that while causes exist, there is no separate birth.
Fourth is the examination through refutation and corroboration;
fifth is the conclusion that returns to the correct meaning.
Within the former, a general formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows:
The dharmas of the future world are definitely non-existent, because they are not subsumed under the present unconditioned [dharmas], just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
As for your statement that "the arising of the future world is definitely existent because it is subsumed under the future, just like future matter," [this is incorrect].
Furthermore, future arising cannot produce [a dharma] because its substance does not exist, like a rabbit's horns and so forth.
Next, the non-existence of present arising is explained.
The opponent says:
Since the Sūtras state that there is the arising of future form and so forth,
we know that there exists a distinct "arising-of-arising" (*jāti-jāti*) which gives rise to all phenomena. If this is so, then...
The *Śāstra* says: "That which is called 'arising,' 'origination,' or 'the present,' up to the point of 'constituting the nature of the present'—
this answers the objection of outsiders who claim that what the Sūtra calls 'arising' must be a distinct, separate entity."
The Sūtra states that there is a "present" which should exist separately from the present; the factors of the present [arise] from the present.
One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
There is no separate productive cause for the production of various forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.
This is because it is stated in the *Sūtra on the Arising of the Three Dharmas of the Present*.
Just as with arising and the present,
there should likewise be a distinct capacity for "presentness" within the present itself.
The *Pratyutpannadharmasūtra* states that arising is subsumed within the three present [factors],
just as your own birth is.
Next, it clarifies that while there is a cause, there is no separate arising.
As stated in the text.
Next, the refutation through progressive and regressive inquiry proceeds;
that is, the formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows.
That which arises apart from form has no separate intrinsic nature external to it,
because its existence is contingent upon the existence of form,
just like form and other such phenomena.
Not so; both would incur the fault of contradicting the thesis (*siddhānta-virodha*).
This was explained in the refutation of the cause of arising.
Tai says: "If there is birth from each and every action,
then since there is a cause for dualistic birth,
there must necessarily be a fruit of dualistic birth."

Since each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) arises without a second dharma, your assertion that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) acts as the cause of arising capable of producing conditioned phenomena is unreasonable.
Jizang states: "For now, I shall first refute the 'small' [notion] of arising."
The "small" [entity] must lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because it is not found within the great, nor within the produced (*janya*) and productive (*janaka*) phenomena, nor within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
etc.; or else, because it is not mentioned, and so forth— these are the two reasons.
Just as with the horns of a rabbit and so forth,
once "small arising" is refuted,
"great arising" is likewise refuted.
You claim that "great arising" (mahābhūta) is the cause of the arising of non-dharmas,
because you say it is capable of producing dharmas;
thus, arising is like [the categories of] smallness and so forth.
Therefore, for him to undergo two births would be a great error.
Since even a single birth is not permitted,
what need is there for two?
That which is "born" is a minor birth because it arises from conditions;
that which is "capable of giving birth" is a major birth because it can give birth to others.
This concludes the correct meaning.
As in the text.
The second section resolves the objection;
the text is divided into two parts.
Initially, the four characteristics are combined into two:
that which arises from the future is called "about to arise," and that which is currently arising is "presently arising."
Among those that are ceasing:
those in the present are about to cease;
those in the past are currently ceasing.
Therefore, when discussing arising, it refers to that which is about to arise;
when discussing cessation, it refers to that which is currently ceasing.
These discussions also mutually clarify one another.
In the Sūtras, there is only mention of arising and ceasing.
Based on this, the Sthavira school uses it as proof that the mind has only two characteristics,
whereas form and other phenomena possess three characteristics.
Next, the general explanation:
among the three characteristics of the conditioned, one contemplates arising and ceasing;
as for the statement that "staying and change are manifested by co-arising," it means:
Because the characteristics of abiding and change are explained in relation to the meaning of arising;
one observes abiding and change precisely at the time of observing arising.
Furthermore, observing both arising and ceasing can give rise to revulsion and detachment.
This passage clearly states that only the two characteristics of arising and ceasing constitute the characteristic of impermanence;
the inclusion of the names "abiding" and "alteration" constitutes the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
The third section clarifies the distinctions in the names and meanings of these four characteristics.
There are eleven types of birth-differences.
The first, entering the womb, is called inferior birth;
in this case, all three stages are inverted.
Regarding the middle two types of entry into the womb,
those who are born from a womb enter and exit without inversion;
Pratyekabuddhas likewise enter and dwell [in the womb] without inversion.
Regarding the statement that "the final entry into the womb is called 'supremely wondrous birth,' for at the three times there is no inversion;
this refers to the Tathāgata":
These characteristics of birth, aging, and death are explained in detail in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Within impermanence, there is the impermanence of arising;
at the time of arising—
Why is it that there is no destruction within arising?
It is because at the time of the characteristic of cessation, this [arising] exists; and this has two types.
First, impermanence of characteristics;
second, impermanence of substance.
The arising of the substance is impermanence.
The dharma of arising fundamentally relies upon the dharma of existence;
therefore, the dharma of cessation is not arising.
One should resolve this difficulty.
This can be understood through reflection.
