"Changeable impermanence" refers to the spontaneous destruction of what is cherished.
Regarding such things as disintegration, impermanence, and being plundered by others:
when non-Buddhists feel weary of and detached from only a portion of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and cannot reach ultimate realization, it is because,
although they have developed a degree of fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) toward material requisites, [they do not apply this to all phenomena].
One cannot be satisfied with the existence and the means of existence.

Next, the attainment of maturation is explained: briefly stated, the causes that bring about the gathering and intensification of the conditions for birth are called "attainment" (*prāpti*), and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "those who have attained maturation" refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
this is based on what is newly acquired; however,
"attainment" (siddhi) encompasses both the new and the old.
In the Mahāyāna, this meaning is general. Ji says:

"This refers to establishing 'acquisition' (prāpti) by naming it the cause of intensification, based on the functional capacity of seeds to produce fruit when they have not yet been suppressed or severed."
Attainment (*prāpti*) does not consist in the seeds having already been suppressed and severed;

therefore, the subsequent passage states: "If they have not yet been suppressed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or suppressed by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), such as the seeds of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that were suppressed by false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)."
Because "maturation" (paripāka) is termed "attainment" (prāpti),
once that [defilement] has been suppressed and abandoned,
it is merely called a "seed" (bīja) and is no longer called an "attainment."
As it says in the Abhidharma regarding the three kinds of maturation:
if one attains the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the form or formless realms while remaining in the desire realm,
the seeds of the desire realm are said to be both mature and immature.
Because it is comprised within the antidote that permanently destroys the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, there are two meanings of "maturation": first, maturation of the basis (*āśraya-paripāka*), which occurs when one has already become free from desire.
Because it possesses substantiality, it is also called "maturation.
Second is the maturation of functional capacity,
such as the capacity for the fruit of non-arising in one who has already abandoned desire.
This is termed "immature.
Here, it is called immature specifically because it lacks the functional capacity to produce a fruit;
however, in terms of its actual substantial existence, it is also termed "mature."
This is based on the predominance of the seeds;
the terminology is the same as for the manifest [state],
and it is also called "maturation."
The subsequent passage states, "There is mastery within the seeds.
This text refers to the preeminent case.
If one were to obtain this dharma from a prior non-arising, then since there would be no acquisition (prāpti) that acts as its cause of arising, it would follow that it never arises and so forth.
For example, Reverend Yung, since ordinary beings have not yet attained that untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*),
they lack the "attainment" (*prāpti*) that serves as the cause for the arising of the noble path;
thus, such a noble path ought not to arise.
Because there would be no cause, one should formulate the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"The noble path within one's own continuum should never arise."
Because there would be no cause;
just as a sprout will not grow without a seed.
Kuiji says: "This objection—that untainted seeds originally do not exist—is further addressed from the perspective of external schools."
It is not that seeds were originally non-existent within the Mahāyāna;
this is the position of the master Vasumitra.
According to this passage, then, untainted seeds were originally non-existent.
If these dharmas were not subject to causes of separation, they would even have to manifest simultaneously.
Jing says: "According to the tenets of the Hīnayāna, the six consciousnesses do not function concurrently;
within a single consciousness, the three natures do not arise together."
Therefore, this objection is raised. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"At the time when a virtuous mind arises, it arises simultaneously in association with minds of the other two natures."
Because they possess causes,
just like a wholesome mind;
even up to an indeterminate mind, when another mind of a different nature arises, it must necessarily arise simultaneously.
Because there is a cause,
it is like an indeterminate mind;
these two preceding phrases correspond to the maturation of the seeds.
Regarding the phrase "if, within the conditions for elicitation, there is mastery over power and so forth," Jing says:
"The seeds of preparatory wholesome karma, as well as a portion of the seeds of the indeterminate, which are wholesome only by way of habituation,
are elicited when they encounter conditions."
The mastery over power is conventionally designated as "attainment"; that is,
it is the attainment of mastery.
Having taken this mastery as the basis, the following clarifies the maturation of manifest activity.
Jì (基) states that, according to this text, it refers to "mastery over power within the conditions for elicitation" (*ākṣepa-pratyaya*).
"Regarding the statement, 'One should know that this attainment is briefly of three kinds,' [Master] Jing says:
'If the seeds of defilement are permanently destroyed...'"
It is also said that even the seeds of the wholesome and the neutral are termed "harmful.
Furthermore, it is stated:
"Hitherto, teachers of the Hīnayāna have mostly explained this solely according to the literal meaning."
While abiding in a lower stage, one can give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth belonging to a higher stage;
this is the case with the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear.
Furthermore, after a neutral mind of deportment arises from a pure meditative concentration, [one may likewise give rise to such a wholesome mind].
Thus, one cannot immediately enter a pure meditative absorption (*śuddhaka-samādhi*).
This is because one must first enter the wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) of a higher stage before entering the pure absorption.
Furthermore, according to the sequence for emerging from absorption, this process continues up to the thought of non-emergence (*an-abhyutthāna-saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, within the category of innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), one may again enter [the meditative absorptions] in reverse order, and so forth. Moreover, according to the [Abhidharma],
an Arhat may fall back and give rise to afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Since there is no meditative absorption of the "receding" type (*hāna-bhāgīya*), from what kind of mind could afflictions arise?
Based on these principles,

one should understand accordingly that when one is in a lower stage, one can attain the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) of a higher stage through the attainment of detachment from that higher stage.
Now, there is likewise no such textual passage in the Mahāyāna.
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"The supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear."
It is not the indeterminate state of deportment (airyāpathika),
but rather the fruition of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala).
Furthermore, it occurs when transcending the dhyānas.
From the first dhyāna, one proceeds in succession up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
remaining there for a long time,
or alternatively, turning toward other forms of contemplation.
This is called "direct entry.
Subsequently, one relies on the fundamental contemplation;
finally, one enters the lower meditative absorption in reverse order.
This is called "entering in reverse.
Through such phrases as "forward and reverse" or "reverse and forward," all logical principles are established.
It is not necessarily required that [the defilement] arise in a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) for it to be established.
An Arhat who has transcended the meditative absorptions may fall back and give rise to the defilements of the formless realm;
from a state of abiding in meditative concentration (*sthiti-bhāgīya-samādhi*), they enter into those defilements.
According to this interpretation,
one whose body resides in a lower stage does not give rise to the wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) belonging to a higher stage.
Tai states that there are three types of acquisition.
The first type of seed is the "attainer," for which the dharmas of the three natures that are to arise constitute the "attained.
The second is the skillful seed of transformation, which serves as the "attainer."
One should employ skillful means to bring about the attainment of transformed indeterminate minds and so forth;
all of these are acquisitions prior to the dharmas themselves.
Third, it is the actual manifestation of the aforementioned various dharmas that constitutes the acquisition.
That is to say, the preceding seeds and the dharmas they have acquired are both termed "active acquisition" (*samudācāra-prāpti*).

These are all cases where one acquires various dharmas by means of "acquisition. If, however, the various [dharmas] that have arisen manifestly are taken as what is acquired, [then the acquisition of those is termed active acquisition].
That which functions to subsume the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is what constitutes "attainment" (prāpti).
This is precisely the attainment of subsequent existence (punarbhava-prāpti).
Furthermore, because the seeds manifest, this is also the attainment of actualized activity (samudācāra-prāpti).
Furthermore, if one takes the preceding seed from the subsequent seed,
this too is explained as the maturation of the seed and the maturation of its manifestation.
Master Ji says: "That which has not yet been definitively subdued, etc., is called 'maturation,' etc.
This is based on the fact that it is the functional capacity (*śakti*) that is immature, not the substance (*dravya*).
The Abhidharma states:
If one attains the untainted path of counteraction (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*), it is then called the maturation of seeds; otherwise, it is called non-maturation.

This applies whether one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, or even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In these cases, that which is not yet matured is likewise termed non-maturation.
What is the nature of this [non-acquisition]?
How can there now be a distinct non-acquisition?
Does non-acquisition encompass all instances of non-acquisition exhaustively?
However, what is the intention behind not establishing [these categories] now?
First, it is to avoid prolixity;
otherwise, one would also have to establish "non-homogeneity" (*asabhāga*), "non-transmigration," and so forth.
Therefore, it will not be discussed in detail here;
furthermore, it is subsumed within the attainment of the middle [state],
as in the case of arising when one is not yet matured.
Both necessarily possess acquisition (*prāpti*).
Since there is no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) for that which is already acquired, it is not mentioned.
The reason it is not said that they attain only a minor degree is that in the Mahāyāna, there is no fault of being burdened by false designations;
the four characteristics are likewise so.
However, the attainment of cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is also common to both the outflowing (sāsrava) and non-outflowing (anāsrava) according to the Mahāyāna;
it is exclusively neutral (avyākṛta) and wholesome (kuśala).
The wholesome is obtained within the Buddha-body.
Now, regarding the Mahāyāna, there exists a seed that cannot be obtained; based upon its support, one establishes the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because the function of the seed lacks the necessary conditions and thus does not produce a subsequent fruit, this is termed "non-analytical."
Why is this attainment established upon its basis?
Because if the body of a Tathāgata were without seeds, it would belong to that basis; therefore, one seeks both the basis and the seeds.
Because seeds that are untainted cannot produce tainted fruits,
this is also the acquisition (*prāpti*) of untainted analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is exclusively the acquisition of untainted analytical cessation, and exclusively the acquisition of non-analytical [cessation] which is untainted.

It encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The wholesome refers to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*);
it is also termed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) pertains to both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) dharmas;
it may arise prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with those dharmas. However, when analyzed specifically, it arises only simultaneously with the dharma.
Regarding the portion of indeterminate [states] within the category of mastery and maturation,
the Abhidharma states:
"The minds of craftsmanship, transformation, and so forth."
Because it arises from the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of one who has thoroughly cultivated the deportments (*īryāpatha*) by means of equalizing [the mind] within equality,
the characteristics are first explained in general within the exposition of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The subsequent section clarifies five pairs of distinctions.
The Tripitaka Master states:
"It is established that the *ālayavijñāna* alone constitutes the total retribution (*vipāka*)."
This contradicts the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
which states that the six sense bases are determined at the time of their abiding. Furthermore,
according to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*) and is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*).
As for the Abhidharma statement that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is "unspecified by nature" (svabhāva-avyākṛta),
this refers to the fact that it is exclusively one type of unspecified [result]:
it is unspecified according to its essential substance (dravya).
It is also termed "neutral by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
However, while "neutral as maturation" (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) is narrow, applying only to the ālayavijñāna,
"neutral by intrinsic nature" is broad in scope.
Regarding those things whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) according to the Abhidharma:

these are the five sense faculties, the three [external] objects, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), and the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
Furthermore, the Abhidharma states:
Regarding "innate indeterminate" (*upapatti-lābhika-avyākṛta*):
that which is the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by unwholesome or wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas is called innate indeterminate.

This refers specifically to the state of birth in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). Why is it not established as a faculty (*indriya*), such as the minor life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) and the major life-faculty, in the same manner as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth?
Now, there is no contradiction in the Mahāyāna not establishing [the faculties] in this way.
Since the Abhidharma establishes them in relation to the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class),
it is known that they pertain to both general and specific faculties.
What is referred to as "produced by prior karma" refers exclusively to the ripened (*vipāka*) result and does not extend to the nurtured (*aupacayika*) or the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
However, when the term "established within a commonality of beings" (*nikāyasabhāga*) is used, it appears to extend to the nurtured as well.
However, it is also said that this is due to prior karma;
therefore, it is solely retribution. Yet, this is not so.
It is established solely upon the mind;
thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that the resultant consciousness (*vipākaja-citta*) of the six consciousnesses can maintain the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of the mind.
The rest is as explained in the *Abhidharma*.
Furthermore, regarding the "subsequent retribution" (paścātkarma) of sentient beings, it is not called "retribution" [in the sense of karmic fruition] nor is it "present"; rather,
it is like the transformation and moistening of birth (pariṇāmopapatti).
Furthermore, when Arhats relinquish their robes and alms bowls to prolong their lives,
these are all results of past karma; therefore,
they are not retributions for the present life.
Question: Is this past karma long or short?
If it were long, it should arise of its own accord; why would it require nourishment?
If [the life span] is short, why is it extended?
Since it is summoned by present karma, it ought to be a retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Now I shall explain the past karma of one's former existences;
today, one nourishes that ancient karma.
Therefore, it is not a result experienced in the present life. Since there are present faculties, by what means is this determined?
Within the text, there is mention of "prior karma."
Therefore, it is not a result experienced in the present life.
In the subsequent clarification of transformation through one's own power,
since it mentions "Arhats and so forth," [it follows that this applies to them].
Thus, we know that the first three fruits all permit the prolongation of life.
The Tripitaka Master says:
"According to the principles of the Mahāyāna..."
The supreme meditative absorption of the limit (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna) pervades all four dhyānas; therefore,
noble ones who have attained any of the four fruits are all able to prolong their life-span.
Regarding the "homogeneity of beings" (nikāyasabhāga), Jing says that its substance consists of the three categories of realms, destinies, and births,
all of which are maturation (vipāka).
The remaining [factors] pertain to all three natures—
defiled, undefiled, and neutral—
and are established solely on the basis of the commonality of sentient beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The same applies to the *Vibhāṣā*.
It was only with the later masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* that the "homogeneity of existing phenomena" (*sabhāgatā*) was first established.
Master Ji says that the "homogeneous character" (nikāyasabhāga) includes both the nurtured (aupacayika) and the outflowing (naiṣyandika), as well as the retributive (vipākaja);
furthermore, it encompasses all three moral natures.

Regarding the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*): Jing says that the seeds of afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), while still bound by all fetters, are conventionally designated as the nature of an ordinary person,
because they obstruct the initial entry into the state of a noble one (*ārya*).

According to reason, the afflictions, karma, and their maturation that are abandoned through seeing should all be established as constituting the essence of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). However,
because it is the seeds that persist in constant succession, it is specifically established based on their maturation.
Tài says: "The various realms of rebirth and destinies each grasp different objects;
this efficacy arises from the delusions of view.
Therefore, regarding the delusions of view..."
Therefore, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is conventionally established upon the functional capacity of the seeds of the afflictions of view.
Noble ones do not undergo rebirth as ordinary beings within the five destinies,
and they realize that [the ultimate] truth is non-different [from their own realization].
Therefore, from the first moment of the path of seeing onward,
one is said to have abandoned the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). As for "integration" (*saṃnipāta*):
Jingyun stated that because they accomplish the same task,
both the Abhidharma and the Yogācāra do not understand or harmonize with the nature of non-concordance.
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
However, the nature of non-conjunction (*aprāpti*) is merely a provisional designation established upon the basis of causes and effects that are separated;
outside of the fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) of the Sarvāstivāda school,
they separately establish the existence of a distinct nature of conjunction (*prāpti*).
That which is called "concordant" and "discordant" refers precisely to the nature of non-attainment and non-maturation.
Within this non-attainment, the non-attaining nature of all phenomena is universally subsumed.
That is to say: the nature of an ordinary person,
the nature of regression,
and the faculties of obstruction.
There is no harmony; it is because of the nature of non-concordance [that contact does not exist].
For contact is able to further harmonize these three factors.
The preceding section clarifies the conditions for the conjunction of that contact;
the following section clarifies its distinctions.
There are those who maintain that the experience of conjunction refers to contact conditioned by the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
That is to say, the six sense bases serve as the condition for contact.
Contact makes contact with the preceding object;
it is also called "reception" (vedanā) and "reception of conjunction."
Either with form and so forth as conditions,
or with the six objects such as form as conditions for contact,
or with attention and so forth as conditions.
"Contact arises conditioned by attention and so forth," or "feeling is conditioned by contact":
next, these conditions for contact and feeling are explained.
Feeling produced with conditions is collectively termed "the harmony of experiencing.
That which is called "the harmony of experiencing conditioned by the six sense bases" refers to this.
Contact is the condition for feeling and is also termed "experiencing.
Since it is now explained that the six sense bases are the condition for contact,
the meaning of the conjunction of experiencing is provisionally established with reference to the six sense bases.
The remaining cases should be understood by analogy.
Alternatively, there is "pure concordance," which refers to the gathering of the twelve types of conditions free from adversity.
In the fifteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma-kośa*, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Freedoms* (*Dvādaśakṣaṇasūtra*) is cited to explain the characteristics of this induction.
First, two propositions are established:
first, self-perfection;
second, perfection of others.
Each of these has two [aspects], making five phrases;
when combined both collectively and individually, they are called twelve.
The Tripitaka Master said:
Consulting the *Śrāvakabhūmi*,
I shall first distinguish their characteristics among the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
The subsequent section clarifies the distinctions.

Regarding the "provisional designation of intrinsic nature" and the "provisional designation of specific characteristics," Jing states that these are not the specific characteristics of the categories of the self-characteristic and the common characteristic.
Because the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are by nature free from names and expressions and are thus inexpressible,
what is here called "intrinsic characteristic" is as follows:
However, within the context of the distinct gates of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena,
"intrinsic nature" refers to the general description of the essential body of all phenomena; therefore,
it is called the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "establishing mere conceptualization in accordance with discourse based on the pervasive, the many, and the few":
because the mind that gives rise to speech arises,
one engages in discourse by universally discriminating the essential characteristics of all phenomena.
When verbal expression arises, one provisionally establishes names based upon that very expression.
Names arise from conceptualization (saṃjñā); they are termed "conceptualization" because they proceed from causes.
Master Ji says: "Because a single entity is perceived through its aspects, there are two distinctions:
self-nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Self-nature is the essence (*tattva*)."
"Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) means "form" (ākṛti);
it refers to the meaning of the essential form of all phenomena (dharma).
What is a "phrase-group" (padakāya)?

Regarding the phrase "that which is designated as the various distinctions of all phenomena based upon their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)," when distinguishing these according to the phenomena themselves,
it is like the general designation of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) or "mind" (*citta*).
Having thus explained its specific characteristics, it is further stated that all gains and losses pertaining to the complete purity of this mind arise from it.
Therefore, the practitioner should ensure that no evil is done by the mind and that all good is practiced.
To clarify this distinction:
regarding the statement that "the phoneme-body (vyañjana-kāya) is the basis for both," a "phoneme" (vyañjana) refers to a syllable (akṣara).
A "syllable" (*akṣara*) has the meaning of being immovable and fixed;
if it is explained as a "grapheme," it has the meaning of making something manifest.
Because these syllables serve as the basis for those names and phrases to clearly express and manifest phenomena,
there are three distinctions explained below.
First, regarding the "abbreviated within the extensive" concerning the expressed meaning:
Phrases (*vyañjana*) are not the primary means of expression;
they merely assist names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*) to constitute expressive communication. They possess remote meanings beyond themselves, gradually diminish in substance, and are abbreviated.
Names, however, express only the essence (*svabhāva*); within names, there is only the essence.
A phrase (*pada*) is called "extensive" because it exhaustively expresses both the essence (*svabhāva*) and the function (*kāritra*) of an object;
since a phrase necessarily carries both a name (*nāman*) and a phoneme (*vyañjana*) when it arises,
it is said that the phrase is capable of extensively expressing the entity (*vastu*).
The second [section] concerns the distinctions in the arising of understanding based on conditions.
The third [section] concerns how various designations such as names and phrases arise through reliance on the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*);
therefore, it is said that names and so forth rely upon those five sciences.
Regarding the statement in the *Pravṛtti* [section]: "There may be a flow characterized by sovereign power, namely, the manifestation of dharmas whose seeds have been impaired"—
this means that although the seeds have been impaired,
they still manifest through the force of remaining sovereign power.
Regarding the section on "Correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*), as for the question, "Why are those various dharmas said to be 'equal' (*sama*)?",
T'ai states: "The mutual similarity among those various dharmas is what is meant by 'equality'."
Because they accord with and resemble one another,
they are called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "equality" is the meaning of "association."
Just as a virtuous cause brings about a pleasant fruit,
so too does discourse arise in accordance with their equal correspondence;
furthermore, it is established as an equality of cause and effect to bring about the understanding of sentient beings.
This is called "equal opening and understanding.
Ji says that the term "equal" refers to the fact that the expressive speech and the expressed phenomena are similar; thus they are called "equal."
This [term] "all" applies to all verbal expressions.
"Establishment" (prajñapti) refers to the establishment of resultant phenomena through causes and conditions that do not depend on words.
"Elucidation" (vibhāvanā) refers to the manifestation of profound and secret essential teachings, wherein the expressive designations correspond to that which is expressed.
From conventional expression up to full comprehension,
because the signifier accords with the signified,
it is called "correspondence" (*samyoga*).
Another interpretation is that "same" (tong) means "identical" (tai),
and it is also used as a term for verbal expression.
The designator is established as being in correspondence with its cause;
the designated is in correspondence with its own-characteristic.
The first two are both mundane;
for those who have attained equal realization, they are supramundane, because their dharmas accord with the [supramundane] characteristics.
Regarding the statement "all supreme skillful means," within the sequence [of stages],
what are the eight positions beginning with the infant and the young child?
The various clouds do not correspond to the sequence of the ten periods;
there are eight distinct periods.
The first period, at ten years of age, is the first stage of illness.
Because those under ten years of age are frequently ill,
the twentieth year is their period of physical beauty;
it is at this time that the complexions of both men and women reach their peak.
Beyond this, one perishes.
The thirtieth year is called the stage of complete strength,
because bodily strength has been perfected.
The fortieth year is called the stage of wisdom;
whatever one undertakes, one necessarily deliberates upon extensively.
The fiftieth year is called the stage of mindfulness.
The sixtieth year is the stage where physical strength and vitality decline due to reflecting on one's own gains and losses;
the seventieth year is the stage where wisdom and mindfulness decline.
The eightieth year is called the stage of confusion.
Master Ji states that the first two [stages] are as described in the second fascicle;
here, however, the third is taken as the starting point.
Because there are further stages of the process of gestation beyond that.
Regarding the enumeration, as for why the limit of number is called *asaṃkhyeya*: [it is because it is beyond calculation].
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, among the one hundred and twenty numerical categories,
the one hundred and third is called *asaṃkhyeya*.
However, this is here translated as "limit" (*prānta*).
From this point onward, because it evolves beyond the reach of calculation,
the sixth major section clarifies its seeds.
The text is divided into four parts.
First, the characteristics of seeds are distinguished;
second, the impairment and suppression of seeds are explained;
third, the number of seeds is clarified.
The four explanations establish the seeds within the ālayavijñāna; among these, there are the preceding [explanations] consisting of both the doctrine and the analogy.
At the beginning of the Jingyun era, Ming explained that the perfuming agent and the seed are neither identical nor separate.
This means that it is not the case that there exists some distinct, substantial entity called a "seed" apart from the various formations (*saṃskāra*);
rather, although the seed is produced by means of the perfuming agent, [it is nonetheless not something other than those formations].
If one analyzes the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that act as perfumers, no real seeds exist within each individual part;
this clarifies that [the seed] is not identical [to the phenomenon]. Nor does it exist elsewhere.
It is not that seeds are formed apart from the perfuming agent;
rather, they are not separate from it.
Nevertheless, it is precisely these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise with such a lineage (*gotra*) and so forth.
This clarifies that the seed, in relation to the fruit it produces, is neither identical nor separate.
However, the phrase "namely, the various formations" refers back to the formations that are produced.
Regarding the phrase "such a lineage," this refers to the productive seed;
it follows the seeds of the three natures.
Because the three natures arise as active manifestations,
it is said, "in this manner," and so forth.
To be thus arranged is what is called the seed and is also called the fruit.
This clarifies that the seeds are arranged within the ālayavijñāna;
such seeds are capable of producing these very seeds and are also the fruits of the perfuming agents,
without any mutual confusion.
"Why is this? and below, it explains the absence of confusion.
Tai says: "It is like the *Sarvāstivāda* [treatment of] suffering and its origin."
This is a single entity;
it is spoken of as two because of cause and effect,
yet it is not the same as this [case].
This is the same as the Sautrāntika masters' position that the "appropriating support" (āśrayopādātṛ) is also designated as a "seed" through the process of perfuming (vāsanā).
However, this seed is not necessarily identical to or different from the retributive body (vipākakāya).
They are not confused with one another;
just as grains such as rice and barley possess the capacity to produce sprouts,
yet that capacity is not separate from the barley and so forth.
If one relies on the gateway of the true principle according to the Mahāyāna,
the seeds reside within the ālayavijñāna,
being neither definitively identical to nor different from that consciousness.
According to the principle of concomitant transformation (*anuvartana*),
the seeds reside within the continuum of the body; as for the retribution body (*vipākakāya*), it is indeterminate as to whether it is identical with or distinct from [the continuum].
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states:
"Seeds reside within the substratum (āśraya) and within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
These two passages, relying on the principle of conformative exposition (anuvartana-naya), speak in terms of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).

Bei says: "That all formations (*saṃskāra*) are thus, that their lineages (*gotra*) are thus, and so forth regarding their arising," clarifies that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are not identical with the seeds in terms of their fruit.
"That they are thus arranged, being called both 'seeds' and 'fruits,'" clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is not different from the seeds.
Having finished recounting the explanations of the three preceding masters, Kuiji states:
"The current interpretation is slightly different;
these [explanations] all take the seeds of active manifestation as their basis."
Nor is it in any other place.
The preceding section explains that the seed is not different from the formations (*saṃskāra*);
the following section, beginning with "but rather the formations themselves," [explains further].
This clarifies that the seed and the formations are not identical.
Why? The following section explains and establishes the aforementioned meaning.
For example, regarding grains such as barley and so forth,
the Tripitaka Master says that the meaning here is as follows:
for instance, a single barley sprout is called a "seed" in relation to its subsequent ear.
In the past, that which arises from a seed was called the fruit;
thus, the stalk itself was considered the pericarp, and the seed was also considered the fruit of the prior seed.
Now, this is explained.
From the passage beginning with "For example" down to "nor from any other place," it is clarified that grains such as rice and barley arise from seeds by way of sprouts and stalks;
furthermore, [the seed] is neither identical to nor different from the stalks and so forth which serve as its fruits.
However, when these primary elements (mahābhūta) arise from such a nature and so forth,
it clarifies that this barley or grain, through the power of conditions such as water and soil,
subsequently produces stalks and fruits that are neither identical to nor different [from their prior state].
This analogy is largely consistent with the preceding points.

Just as a seed—such as a stalk or grain—is designated as a "seed" when it serves as the condition for the subsequent production of sprouts and so forth, the knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is likewise so.

This is because the preceding non-associated provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) do not require seeds for their production; thus, they cannot serve as the "external category" required to resolve the objection.

It is said: "In the preceding discussion on causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it was stated that the eighth consciousness serves as the causal condition. How, then, can this [provisional phenomenon] be a seed?"
Therefore, this passage exists.
If it were not so, then this would be the meaning of the combination of identity and difference.
The subsequent response is as follows: after explaining how such [states] are incompatible with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth, he then concludes the preceding section.
Second, regarding the subduing of seeds, there are four propositions concerning their subdual.
Jingyun says: First, there is the habitual defilement;
second, all views taken collectively are termed false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as those held by various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The third [type] is the habituation to wrong views that can sever the roots of goodness.
This text does not specify that it refers only to wrong views that deny suffering and its origin;
rather, it indicates that wrong views pertaining to all four truths sever the roots of goodness.
Fourth, because the seeds of defilement are permanently destroyed at the time of the vajra-like samādhi,
the wholesome dharmas conducive to merit can no longer draw forth their retribution;
this is termed "suppression by impairment."
Master Ji said: "The first phrase refers to those who are sharp but do not apply themselves to the afflictions;
the second phrase refers to those who apply themselves but are not sharp;
the third phrase refers to those who have severed their roots of goodness."

The end of the previous fascicle, in the fourth [section], states: "It is not that the seeds of goodness are damaged and suppressed by an auxiliary associate; rather, it refers to when one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) enters the state of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
This fourth type of entity is called 'damaging the seeds of goodness' because its very nature is non-existent."

The first two [types of harm] cause the seeds of the wholesome to lack power; this is called "damage," but not total non-arising. The third phrase refers to causing the manifest [wholesome] not to arise, whereby the seeds lack efficacy;
this is called "damage" that results in the failure to attain maturation.
It is not that the attainment of the entire substance is non-existent,
as was explained previously in the section on attainment.
Regarding the second phrase, it refers to those who see and cling to false views.
This is the grasping at views;
it is the frequent cultivation of false views; this is false view.
Third, regarding the enumeration of the seeds,
Ki says: "If they are newly perfumed,
how can it be said that if they abide as 'original abiding' (mūla-sthiti), they are called inferior grade?"
The commentary states:
This, too, has been perfumed since beginningless time;
however, it is further prolonged so that it does not give rise to active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
These original seeds are termed "inferior grade" (mṛdu).
After being perfumed, they are termed "middling" (madhya) or "superior" (adhimātra) because they no longer revert to their former state.
[Objection: Since all three grades of seeds are originally present, why is it that only after undergoing cultivation and refinement are they designated as "middling"?
These three kinds of seeds originally all exist inherently. However,
within this context, based on the meaning of a single kind of seed, it is explained that there are three kinds [of functions] such as perfuming (*vāsanā*),
while their essence is one and so forth.
It is not that the three kinds of seeds transform from inferior into middling;
this is called "transformation and cessation."
Because it is of one seed, there is no contradiction in its transformation being uniform.
This [seed] originally exists in three grades;
subsequently, after being perfumed and refined, [it becomes so].
The inferior grade is transformed to equal the middling grade;
therefore, within the Buddha-body, all things are equal,
and there are no seeds of the three grades— superior, middling, or inferior.
In this context, the distinction in names is based on the transformation being complete across three grades;
it does not refer to transformation in a single grade or across three stages.
This is the interpretation of the two masters, the "New" and the "Old."
The fourth section clarifies the establishment of seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
First, it explains the contaminated (*sāsrava*) seeds;
subsequently, it explains the supramundane uncontaminated (*lokottara-anāsrava*) seeds.
The Tripitaka Master says:

Among the five categories, discrimination is the dharma of the mind within the triple world; because it cannot realize the principle of the two kinds of emptiness, it is entirely the false attachment to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The seeds produced by conceptual discrimination are called "habit-energies" (vāsanā).
They encompass all contaminated seeds without exception.
These seeds are substantially real.
In terms of substantial reality, there are various functional distinctions;
because these do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-satya),
they are termed conventionally existent (saṃvṛti-sat).
There are two types of conventional existence (saṃvṛti-sat):
first, in relation to the ālayavijñāna;
second, in relation to that which is produced from it.
The three [aspects] are capable of perfuming;
their characteristics cannot be definitively stated as being either different or non-different.
They are like *tathatā* (suchness), which exists as a real entity, yet is definitely neither identical to nor different from all phenomena (*dharma*).
True suchness (tathatā) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) exist as substantial realities; seeds (bīja) and conventional reality (saṃvṛti-satya) exist as substantial realities.
Although the two truths are distinct, they are identical in their substantial existence.
This is intended to illustrate the principle that all phenomena are neither identical nor different, and so forth;
thus, it is cited as an analogy.
Jing says: "Some treatises state that all seeds are the perfuming of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and discrimination, which is precisely the same as this text."
The minds that are about to realize the three natures are all attachments to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
because they are seeds of the false conceptualization of the *parikalpita*.
Thus says T'ai.
Regarding the statement, "I shall briefly explain the establishment of seeds":
previously, according to the principle of conforming transformation (*anuvartana*),
it was stated that seeds do not exist as distinct, substantial entities separate from the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Now, based on the gateway of ultimate reality, it is said:
"within the ālayavijñāna. Ji (Baoshan Ji) says:
"This is in view of the non-substantiality of the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature)."
This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because it possesses substantial existence, it is said to be real;
it is not like the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is designated as conventionally existent.
Because it is of the nature of universal imagination,
it is called the "universal seed.
Because it is bound by outflows and is stubborn and unyielding, [it is so named].
It is called the "perfuming of names.
Furthermore, because the perfumed seeds universally serve as causes for all phenomena,
they are termed "universal" (sarvatraga).
The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), fascicle 15, states: "This heaviness (*dausthulya*) is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
therefore, it is called 'pervasive' (*sarvatraga*)."
Next, the question and answer provide an explanation to clarify the seeds of the supramundane.

Regarding the statement that "all supramundane dharmas arise from seeds with True Suchness as their objective support (*ālambana*)," Jing and Bei state: "If one follows the school of Saṃghabhadra, which does not posit the existence of innate untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), there are two ways to interpret this passage."
First interpretation:
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized suchness (tathatā),
the twelve divisions of the sūtras flow forth from it in succession and circulate in the world.

Prior to the path of seeing, the aids to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) and the aids to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) arise with the scriptural teachings as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because they are named after their fundamental basis, they are called "arising from the object-condition of true suchness" (*tathatā-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Second, the explanation:

the supramundane noble path of the first stage arises from the "wholesome states conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that follow the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), acting as its predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) and immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Second, it arises from the object-condition of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the interpretation of the text according to Śrīlāta and Dharmapāla, there are also two explanations.
The first states that the originally existent untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
the roots of goodness such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) are able to arise.
Second, it is said that the inherently existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The factors conducive to liberation and so forth serve as the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*);
the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
and suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
The supramundane dharmas of the first stage arise;

however, the treatise explains this from the perspective of the subsequent object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Therefore, it says that all supramundane dharmas arise from the object-condition of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Master Jing subsequently re-examined the commentaries of Dharmapāla and others regarding this passage.
To properly answer the question concerning the causes and conditions,
he replied that [the consciousness] arises from seeds existing from the beginning.
If this habit-energy (vāsanā), which comprises all seeds, is further termed the "pervasive heaviness" (sarvatraga-dauṣṭhulya),
from what seeds do those supramundane dharmas of the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) belonging to the three vehicles arise?
If it is said that the seeds of the heavy and coarse (dauṣṭhulya) are the seeds from which [defiled phenomena] arise, this is not logical.

The following answer explains that all supramundane dharmas arise from the seed of the objective condition of suchness (tathatā-ālambana-pratyaya), and are not produced from seeds accumulated as latencies (vāsanā).
The meaning of the answer clarifies that the paths of seeing (darśanamārga) of the three vehicles arise from seeds existing from the beginning;
these are the direct causes of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) which takes true suchness (tathatā) as its object,
and they now arise from those [seeds].
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] arises from seeds which take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);

it does not arise from seeds accumulated by those [beings] who possess outflows (*sāsrava*). Tai (Tai Xuanzang) states that Master Śīlabhadra established only the theory of newly perfumed seeds (*navasaṃskāra*).
Therefore, suchness is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
When the untainted [state] first arises, it is produced solely from seeds created by correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*).
The initial untainted state does not arise from a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Hugyue and others establish only the perfuming of the fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava-vāsanā*).
This nature of the perfuming of the fundamental existence realizes *tathatā* (suchness);
it is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the perfuming of the fundamental existence.
This perfuming is called the seed of the object-condition of *tathatā* (suchness).
From this, the Path of the Sages first arises.
Master Śīlabhadra established two types of perfuming: the new and the old.
As explained by Ratnacandra and others regarding "previously perfumed":
although there is innate, previously perfumed habituation,
if there were no newly perfumed habituation, [enlightenment would not arise].
Because the old latencies cannot produce the Noble Path,
it is only through the union of the new and the old that the Noble Path can arise. Since the nature of the new and old latencies takes True Suchness as its object-condition,
it is said that supramundane dharmas arise from seeds whose objective condition is True Suchness.
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is taught that the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) and the nature of understanding (*bodhisattvagotra*) are in union, and from this all noble paths arise.

Question: If [all things] are produced from seeds accumulated as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and so forth, up to the point that everything has the suchness (*tathatā*) as its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), then...
Furthermore, there is an objection. The intent of the objection is as follows:
If supramundane phenomena were produced from seeds that have the *tathatā* (suchness) as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), [then...]
If all sentient beings have true suchness (tathatā) as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
then they should all possess seeds that take suchness as their object. How,
then, can one establish the distinction between those who attain parinirvāṇa and those who do not?
The following section, based on the presence or absence of obstructions, reveals whether the supramundane seeds within those bodies are perfected or not;
thus, there are five distinct spiritual lineages (*pañca-gotra*).
As for the statement, "One should know that this is because they are sustained by the power of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)," [it means as follows].
The transformation from an ordinary being into a noble one through the path of seeing of the three vehicles is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
This transformation of the basis is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
With suchness as its objective condition, it sustains the continuous succession of supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) practices.
The Tripitaka Master says:
The second fascicle of the eight-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* distinguishes the five natures,
including the fixed natures of the three vehicles.
For the first three types of persons,
the fourth is those of indeterminate nature,
and the fifth is the icchantika.
There are two types of icchantikas.
The first is the bodhisattva-icchantika,
who ultimately lacks the possibility of attaining buddhahood.
Second, those icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness will certainly attain Buddhahood if they encounter superior conditions;
as for others who have already passed away in the West, [the same applies].
The Sanskrit original of the *Laṅkāvatāra* is likewise the same.
